turns.en: Tell me the history of Muse.
turns.zh: 给我讲讲 Muse 的历史。

turns.en: The first thing to start with is probably what our vision was when we started Meta Super Intelligence Labs. When we started it, Mark published this memo that myself, Nat Friedman, and a bunch of others worked together with him closely on, called Personal Super Intelligence. The whole idea was: how do we make AI, how do we build powerful AI that actually makes all of our lives better? How do we build something that actually lifts the human experience, broadly speaking? In that memo, we spoke to a bunch of ideas and alluded to a lot of what Muse ultimately became, but we were gesturing at it very, very early. This was in June 2025, before agents had happened in any meaningful way. In the summer of 2025, AI was just in a totally different spot. But that's what we wanted to build towards. That was the mission of MSL, and that was where we wanted to take everything.
turns.zh: 首先要说的，可能是我们创办 Meta Super Intelligence Labs 时的愿景。我们创办时，Mark 发表了一份备忘录，是我、Nat Friedman 和其他一些人跟他密切合作写的，叫《个人超级智能》。整个想法就是：我们如何让 AI，如何构建强大的 AI，真正让我们所有人的生活变得更好？我们如何构建某种东西，从广义上真正提升人类体验？在那份备忘录里，我们谈到了很多想法，基本上暗示了 Muse 最终成为的很多东西，但我们当时只是在非常非常早地指向它。那是 2025 年 6 月，在智能体以任何有意义的方式出现之前。2025 年夏天，AI 还处于完全不同的阶段。但那就是我们想要构建的方向。那是 MSL 的使命，也是我们想要把一切带向的地方。

turns.en: Then we just got to work building models, because the end-to-end process of developing any of these frontier models is many, many, many months. You have to build your entire stack, produce the data sets, pre-train the model, then do post-training, and build a whole stack for that. It's a very lengthy end-to-end process. And this whole production line at the start of this year—Opus 4.5 obviously really caused many people, including us, to see what the future of agents could be, and really brought the potential of agents to the foreground. OpenClaw was happening at the start of the year. Nat Friedman, who I work closely with, was I think the first person within MSL to work with OpenClaw and try OpenClaw. He had an experience I would describe as somewhere between terrifying and euphoric. I think he really went all in. He trusted entirely. He's told some of these stories—he had a Stripe Sessions interview where he talked about some of this—where he told his OpenClaw that he wanted to drink more water, and then his OpenClaw would watch him in security footage to make sure he was drinking water and tell him good job. He had many, many crazy stories like this. It also makes you realize, oh, there's something quite magical about what's happening here.
turns.zh: 然后我们就开始着手构建模型，因为开发任何这些前沿模型的端到端过程都要很多很多个月。你必须构建整个技术栈，生产数据集，预训练模型，然后做后训练，还要为此构建一整套技术栈。这是一个非常漫长的端到端过程。而今年年初的这整条生产线——Opus 4.5 显然让很多人，包括我们，看到了智能体的未来可能是什么样，真正把智能体的潜力推到了前台。OpenClaw 在今年年初出现。和我密切合作的 Nat Friedman，我想是 MSL 内部第一个接触 OpenClaw 并尝试 OpenClaw 的人。他的体验，我会形容为介于恐惧和狂喜之间。我觉得他真的全身心投入了。他完全信任。他讲过一些这样的故事——他在一次 Stripe Sessions 采访中谈过一些——他告诉他的 OpenClaw 他想多喝水，然后他的 OpenClaw 会通过监控录像看他，确保他在喝水，并告诉他做得好。他有很多很多这样的疯狂故事。这也让你意识到，哦，这里发生的事情相当神奇。

turns.en: And I remember one of the things that Nat told me—and this is one of the things I remember the most—is he said, 'I think there really is something here.' And I don't know, early adopter Nat Friedman is a pretty good indicator, because he was one of the first customers of Stripe back in the day, and then was really early on a lot of open source developer stuff, and he also helped create GitHub Copilot and many other things. So that was a clear signal. It's like, okay, there's clearly something pretty magical about personal agents generally speaking. But when you actually trust the personal agent and really bring it into your life, it is the ability to do so many things. After hearing all of these crazy stories, I started using it very deeply. I think for many weeks, both of us were sort of like every spare moment we would just spend talking to our OpenClaws and really immersing ourselves in what personal agents could be.
turns.zh: 我记得 Nat 告诉我的一件事——这也是我记得最清楚的事情之一——他说：“我觉得这里真的有些东西。”我不知道，早期采用者 Nat Friedman 是个相当好的指标，因为他当年是 Stripe 最早的客户之一，然后很早就参与了很多开源开发者的事情，他还帮助创建了 GitHub Copilot 和许多其他东西。所以那是一个明确的信号。就像，好吧，个人智能体从广义上讲显然有些相当神奇的东西。但当你真正信任个人智能体，真正把它带入你的生活，它就有能力做这么多事情。听完所有这些疯狂的故事后，我开始非常深入地使用它。我想有好几周，我们俩都是每个空闲时刻都在跟我们的 OpenClaw 对话，真正沉浸在个人智能体可能是什么之中。

turns.en: What was your initial reaction? Euphoria or terror?
turns.zh: 你最初的反应是什么？狂喜还是恐惧？

turns.en: Nat at the time had built this prompt to do basically a full psychoanalysis of yourself. There were multiple waves of deep psychological probing. He basically wrote this prompt for you to use an OpenClaw. And I think that was one of the very first things I did with my own OpenClaw. It was maybe the equivalent of three years of therapy, all compressed into this one moment.
turns.zh: Nat 当时构建了一个提示词，基本上是对你自己做一次完整的心理分析。有多轮深度的心理探查。他基本上写了这个提示词，让你用在 OpenClaw 上。我想那是我用自己的 OpenClaw 做的第一批事情之一。那大概相当于三年的心理治疗，全部压缩到这一刻。

turns.en: Wait, I'm curious why, when you get your first shot at OpenClaw, this is one of the first things you do.
turns.zh: 等等，我很好奇，为什么你第一次拿到 OpenClaw，这是你最先做的事情之一。

turns.en: You know, I downloaded it. I installed it. And then Nat was like, 'Oh, you should do this.' I was like—I was next to him. He was like, 'Okay, I'll just do the thing you're telling me to do.' And then—
turns.zh: 你知道，我下载了它。我安装了它。然后 Nat 说：“哦，你应该做这个。”我当时——我就在他旁边。他说：“好吧，我就做你让我做的事。”然后——

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: And then, you know, this crazy experience.
turns.zh: 然后，你知道，就是这种疯狂的体验。

turns.en: Wait, say more about the crazy experience though.
turns.zh: 等等，再多说说那个疯狂的体验。

turns.en: Oh, well, it was just very intense. I mean, it was like, again, it was like three years of therapy, because it was just successive rounds of deep psychological probing. It had other information about me. It had access to my email and access to a bunch of my photos, and it could go and look up other information and sort of pull it all together. I was very vulnerable through that process.
turns.zh: 哦，嗯，就是非常强烈。我的意思是，又像三年的心理治疗，因为它就是一轮又一轮深度的心理探查。它有我其他的信息。它可以访问我的电子邮件，访问我的一堆照片，它还能去查找其他信息，把这一切拼凑起来。在那个过程中我非常脆弱。

turns.en: This was in February. Both of us, I think, had come to this joint conclusion that this is clearly—there's clearly something really special happening here. And we both wrote memos at that time. I wrote a memo about—and both of these we kind of sent up through the Meta board, because for whatever reason it's board season. I wrote a memo about how I felt that in many ways this was the final consumer product, and that the super agent was something that, as far as consumer products went, was a clear endpoint in many ways. And then he wrote one called—he wrote actually two, which had very memorable lines: 'the clause, the law, and trust is a must,' which ultimately defined a lot of the core of how we built these products. So we came to this conclusion. This was in February. There was something very important here.
turns.zh: 这是二月份的事。我想我们俩都得出了这个共同的结论：这显然——这里显然正在发生一些非常特别的事情。我们当时都写了备忘录。我写了一份关于——这两份我们都通过 Meta 董事会提交了，因为不知为何那正好是董事会季。我写了一份备忘录，谈我觉得这在很多方面是最终的消费产品，而超级智能体就消费产品而言，在很多方面是一个明确的终点。然后他写了一份叫——他实际上写了两份，其中有非常令人难忘的句子：“条款、法律，信任是必须的”，这最终定义了我们构建这些产品的很多核心。所以我们得出了这个结论。这是二月份的事。这里有些非常重要的东西。

turns.en: And then we built our teams, we built a prototype within like a week, maybe two weeks. And demoed it to the board. It was this very fast cycle. And many of the decisions that made their way into the final Muse product were present in the first prototype. The Jollybot was there. The early version of the Muse Charm was in that first—that very first meeting. Not all of the ideas and not all the tabs were there, but a lot of them were present. Then from there, obviously that was February, we launched the product seven months later. It was the really, really hard process of taking this prototype, where it sometimes worked and was magical but most of the time didn't work and would constantly break, and going from there to something that would be highly reliable, like a beautifully crafted consumer product that we felt confident as a contribution to the consumer world. And that was this very lengthy and quite painful process.
turns.zh: 然后我们组建了团队，大概在一周、也许两周内构建了一个原型。并向董事会做了演示。这是一个非常快的周期。最终 Muse 产品中的许多决策都出现在第一个原型里。Jollybot 当时就在。Muse Charm 的早期版本在那第一次——那第一次会议上就有了。不是所有的想法、不是所有的标签页都在，但很多都在。然后从那里开始，显然那是二月份，我们在七个月后发布了产品。那是一个非常非常艰难的过程：把这个原型——它有时能工作、很神奇，但大多数时候不工作、会不断崩溃——变成高度可靠的东西，像一个精心打造的消费产品，让我们有信心作为对消费世界的贡献。那是一个非常漫长且相当痛苦的过程。

ts.sec: Mark's Early Use of the Prototype

turns.en: And before we get there, I want to go back to the idea that you wrote the prototype. You guys created the prototype in like a one to two weeks. You show it to the board. What's Mark's role in all this?
turns.zh: 在聊到那之前，我想回到你写原型这件事上。你们大概用一到两周做出了原型，然后拿给董事会看。马克在这其中扮演了什么角色？

turns.en: He was like experiencing the sort of like euphoria/ terror of the product at the same time as all of us. I think he's talked about this in various interviews, but like I think he he used it for a bunch of things around the home and he was using it with his kids and he used it in his um uh in his MMA training. Like he had it watch videos of his of himself doing MMA training and like it would give him tips on like how to improve. there were like some staff meetings and by the way like you know this kind of became a thing for for much of the the meta team um was like having these having a staff meeting and saying like what were the what were the crazy experiences that you had with um with with your agent again this was back in February. It's very interesting to kind of um think back to this whole cycle because obviously the openclaw phenomena it peaked and then disappeared. Yeah, there were, you know, it didn't it didn't persist and and I think a lot of people kind of had this experience which was it was just like you'd have these magic moments but for the most part didn't like work that well and there were all these problems and then you know it just kind of like died down and so part of I think the building the product a lot of the focus of the product was just like how do you make this into an actual reliable consumer experience that you feel comfortable putting in front of over time billions of people and you can feel confident that like most of those people have an amazing experience.
turns.zh: 他和我们所有人一样，体验到了这个产品带来的那种狂喜与恐惧。我想他在各种采访里都谈过，他把它用在了家里的一堆事情上，和孩子们一起用，还用在综合格斗训练里。他让它看自己训练综合格斗的视频，然后它会给他改进建议。还有一些员工会议，顺便说一句，这后来成了 Meta 团队很多人的一种习惯，就是开员工会议时问，你和你的智能体有过什么疯狂的经历。再说一次，这是二月份的事了。回头想这整个周期非常有意思，因为 OpenClaw 现象显然达到顶峰后就消失了。是的，它没有持续下去，我想很多人都有这种体验：你会有一些神奇时刻，但大多数时候它并不那么好用，有各种各样的问题，然后就慢慢沉寂了。所以我认为，构建这个产品，很大一部分重点就是，如何把它变成一个真正可靠的消费级体验，让你放心地把它呈现在数十亿人面前，并且有信心其中大多数人都会有很棒的体验。

ts.sec: Why Muse Succeeded Where OpenClaw Didn't

turns.en: Why were you able to do that and the developers open call were not?
turns.zh: 为什么你们能做到，而 OpenClaw 的开发者们做不到？

turns.en: Well, first of all, I think we respect Peter Seinberger and everyone who's contributed to OpenClaw immensely. Like I think Peter is definitely a visionary. I think whatever happened in his beautiful brain that created OpenClaw is magical. And I think maybe the unglamorous part of what made made Muse so magical was just really grinding out and sanding out all of the details to make the combined model plus product experience really amazing and we did many many iterations on the model itself. We aimed the overall model roadmap towards building towards personal super intelligence broadly speaking but certainly personal agents as like
turns.zh: 首先，我们极其尊重 Peter Seinberger 以及所有为 OpenClaw 做出贡献的人。我认为 Peter 绝对是个有远见的人。他那颗漂亮的脑袋里发生的、创造出 OpenClaw 的一切，是神奇的。而让 Muse 如此神奇的，或许是不那么光鲜的部分，就是真正地死磕、打磨所有细节，让模型加产品的整体体验变得非常出色，我们在模型本身上做了很多很多次迭代。我们把整体的模型路线图瞄准了构建个人超级智能，宽泛地说，但肯定是个人智能体，就像——

turns.en: Say more about that and how that differentiates between your other competitors.
turns.zh: 再多讲讲这个，以及它如何让你和其他竞争对手区分开来。

turns.en: Yeah. Well, this is this is kind of
turns.zh: 好。这个，这有点——

turns.en: That's actually really interesting.
turns.zh: 这其实真的很有意思。

turns.en: Yeah. It's actually useful to go back to the moment because if you go back to the start of the year, February, Opus and Claude were way ahead in coding, way ahead of anyone else and they were exploding. It was the beginning of the sort of like you know Anthropic takeover in the whole industry and it was a very scary moment I think generally speaking which is like oh wow this is you know they're so ahead on coding and and then obviously they had mythos and you know they were they had like this clear lead. I think the the conventional wisdom in the industry was that coding agents were the only form factor that mattered or maybe the only technology that mattered or only the only capability that mattered for advanced AI. you know there's this incredible force in the industry to just like go and crowd that use case and compete with Anthropic on coding agents because of our experiences and our conviction that I think formed around this idea of personal agents and the sort of taking a step back I think the reason why we did personal super intelligence in the first place was that it was also what we believed meta was uniquely positioned to do and we can talk more about that but like I think because of that
turns.zh: 是的。回到那个时刻其实很有用，因为如果你回到今年年初，二月份，Opus 和 Claude 在编程上遥遥领先，远远超过其他任何人，而且正在爆发式增长。那是整个行业被 Anthropic 接管的开端，我认为总的来说那是一个非常可怕的时刻，就是，哇，他们在编程上领先这么多，然后显然他们有了 Mythos，他们有着明显的领先优势。我认为行业里的传统智慧是，编程智能体是唯一重要的形态，或者也许是唯一重要的技术，或者唯一重要的能力，对于先进 AI 而言。行业里有一股巨大的力量，就是去涌入那个用例，在编程智能体上与 Anthropic 竞争。但因为我们自己的经历和信念，我们形成了围绕个人智能体的想法。退一步说，我认为我们当初做个人超级智能的原因是，我们也相信这是 Meta 拥有独特定位去做的事，我们可以多聊聊这个，但我觉得正因为如此——

turns.en: Well, let's talk about that now.
turns.zh: 好，那我们现在就聊聊这个。

turns.en: Okay, we'll just do do the weave. I think one of the first things I told Mark even before the whole scale and meta deal happened and and everything, one of the first things I told him was I think Meta is actually a really special company if we have AGI or ASI or whatever you want to call it. Because part of the promise of AI is that for all of us, we have a mix of things that we want to do and things that we have to do. And the promise of AGI is that we're going to spend almost none of the time doing things that we have to do because the AIS will just start doing a lot of that for us and we can spend all of our time on things that we want to do. And for me, Meta's products represent the things that we all want to do. Like my use of Instagram or WhatsApp or Facebook like these are products that represent what I, you know, I follow my interests. I follow my hobbies. I follow all people that I like my friends and the people I care about like the product span of meta encapsulates the sort of like what we want to spend our times doing sort of realm. I think on a long arc meta is an incredible winner through all this. That's like one of the first things that I believed about meta and super intelligence. And then ultimately a lot of those ideas made its way into this concept of personal super intelligence. You know, you can kind of look at it a few ways. One is what's the heritage of the company? The heritage of meta is connecting people with their friends and family. Um, helping them discover their interests. Like these are things that are very human. And then there's also the sort of like you can take the business lens which is Meta has distribution to three and a half billion people using the apps every day. And the natural area where Meadow was going to be successful is consumer AI.
turns.zh: 好，我们就这么交织着聊。我想，甚至在 Scale 和 Meta 的交易发生之前，我最早告诉马克的事情之一就是，我认为如果我们有了 AGI 或 ASI，或者不管你想叫它什么，Meta 其实是一家非常特别的公司。因为 AI 的承诺的一部分是，对我们所有人来说，我们想做的事和必须做的事是混合在一起的。而 AGI 的承诺是，我们将几乎不花时间在必须做的事上，因为 AI 会开始替我们做很多这样的事，我们可以把所有时间花在想做的事上。对我来说，Meta 的产品代表的就是我们所有人都想做的事。比如我用 Instagram、WhatsApp 或 Facebook，这些产品代表的是我追随自己的兴趣、爱好，追随我喜欢的朋友和我关心的人。Meta 的产品跨度囊括了我们想花时间去做的那类事情。我认为从长远来看，Meta 会是这一切中的巨大赢家。这是我最初相信的关于 Meta 和超级智能的事情之一。最终，很多这些想法都融入了个人超级智能这个概念。你可以从几个角度看。一个是公司的传承是什么？Meta 的传承是把人们与朋友和家人连接起来，帮助他们发现自己的兴趣。这些都是非常人性的事。然后你也可以从商业角度看，Meta 拥有每天 35 亿人使用其应用的触达。而 Meadow 自然会取得成功的领域是消费级 AI。

turns.en: It's not work. It's not coding. It's personal.
turns.zh: 不是工作，不是编程，是个人化的。

turns.en: Yeah. Exactly. So personal agents and personal AI and and consumer AI, broadly speaking, were always the zones where we always felt that Meta was going to do some be able to do something very special. So that brings us to uh okay, early 2026. Now you have the prototype, you have the buy in, everybody knows Mark's on board and now you're doing the seven months of the difficult work of refining this product.
turns.zh: 对，没错。所以个人智能体、个人 AI 和消费级 AI，宽泛地说，一直是我们觉得 Meta 能够做出非常特别的东西的领域。这就把我们带到了，好，2026 年初。现在你有了原型，你有了支持，所有人都知道马克加入了，然后你开始了七个月的艰难工作，打磨这个产品。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: There was kind of the spectre which was like oh personal agents like they came and went and we always felt that it was because you know the the experience wasn't perfect. It wasn't polished yet you know all that kind of stuff. But like we knew that that was something that we had to like think about as you know as we were developing this product. We focused our model development road map. The top focus uh or one of the top focuses was towards building on personal agents and we had like these long spreadsheets of hundreds or even thousands of different not thousands but but more than a hundred like specific behaviors and capabilities that we knew the model needed to have to be able to build the ideal personal agent. Like it was very very meticulous.
turns.zh: 有一种阴影，就是，哦，个人智能体，它们来了又走了，我们一直觉得那是因为体验不够完美，还没打磨好，诸如此类。但我们知道，在开发这个产品时，这是我们必须考虑的事情。我们聚焦了模型开发的路线图。最核心的焦点，或者说最核心的焦点之一，就是构建个人智能体。我们有长长的电子表格，列着数百甚至数千种不同的——不是数千，而是超过一百种具体的行为和能力，我们知道模型必须具备这些才能构建出理想的个人智能体。非常非常细致。

turns.en: And then over time we built evals for all of those. We figured out how to train the model to be really really good at every single one of those things. And we have these reviews where we like look at that spreadsheet and we figure out the things that we're bad at and make sure that we're improving on them. Like we did this like very meticulous process to slowly just keep improving and sanding out all the edges of the model so that it could power the product.
turns.zh: 然后随着时间推移，我们为所有这些方面建立了评估。我们弄清楚了如何训练模型，让它在每一项上都表现得非常非常出色。我们还有这些评审，我们会查看那个电子表格，找出我们做得不好的地方，并确保我们不断改进。我们做了这样一个非常细致的过程，慢慢地不断改进，打磨掉模型的所有棱角，以便它能驱动产品。

turns.en: Is that really the culture of Meta too? This like constant like sanding of the products?
turns.zh: 这也是 Meta 的文化吗？这种不断打磨产品的文化？

turns.en: Yeah. A lot of the culture of Meta is like once you know what you're measuring, there's very talented people and you can optimize for those things, you can send out all the details, you can make those things amazing. turns.en: I think it's all right.
turns.zh: 我认为这没问题。

turns.en: I think one of the magical things about Muse was that we really took quite a bit of time to sweat all the details before ultimately coming out with a product. Because I think that personal agents was one of these product areas that kind of rested on a knife's edge: if it can reliably deliver these magical experiences, it has the potential to be one of the greatest consumer products ever. But you're dealing with models, you're dealing with something nondeterministic, you're dealing with agents—they can break, they can be unreliable. If people have these unreliable experiences, they think it's trash. It was one of these things where getting the product to a point of quality and value such that it resonated with so many of the people who downloaded and used it.
turns.zh: 我认为 Muse 的神奇之处之一在于，我们真的花了相当多的时间打磨所有细节，才最终推出产品。因为我认为个人智能体是那种如履薄冰的产品领域：如果它能可靠地提供这些神奇体验，它就有可能成为有史以来最伟大的消费产品之一。但你面对的是模型，是不确定的东西，是智能体——它们可能崩溃，可能不可靠。如果人们遇到这些不可靠的体验，他们会觉得这是垃圾。所以关键是要把产品做到一定的质量和价值，让它能引起那么多下载和使用它的人的共鸣。

turns.en: I want to talk more about this process. I'm curious how much resources, how big the team, how many people working on it. Do you guys have any data on like okay I'm using Muse nine great experiences two like inconsistent or you know shitty experiences and then I turn out like do you have any information on this?
turns.zh: 我想多聊聊这个过程。我很好奇投入了多少资源，团队有多大，有多少人在做这个。你们有没有数据，比如我用 Muse 有九次很棒的体验，两次不太稳定或者很糟糕的体验，然后我就流失了？你们有这方面的信息吗？

turns.en: You can see this from a lot of the other agent products at the start of the year—like almost everyone turned out of those and it's because they were unreliable. We did a lot of user testing of Muse. We did many many rounds of new people trying to download it and use it from scratch and just seeing what that experience was like. A huge part of the premise of Muse and I think what's really landed is that it is a different thing from what most people have experienced with consumer AI. It is not a chatbot. It is an agent and it can do agent things for you. And I think to a developer this is kind of old news because they've had to download agents and have been using them for a while. But for most people, just even that graduation process needs to be explained and needs to be onboarded in a very thoughtful way. And then for sure we definitely have seen—because we've done tests with different versions of the model and various model versions and continuously do those AB tests—the product experience is very very sensitive to model quality. It's very sensitive to how reliably the models can undergo these tasks, how reliably they communicate with the user about them, how reliably they check back with the user if there's things that they require guidance on.
turns.zh: 你可以从今年年初很多其他智能体产品上看到这一点——几乎所有人都流失了，就是因为它们不可靠。我们对 Muse 做了大量用户测试。我们做了很多很多轮，让新用户尝试下载并从头开始使用，看看体验如何。Muse 的一个核心前提，我认为也是它真正成功的地方，就是它和大多数人体验过的消费级 AI 不同。它不是聊天机器人。它是一个智能体，可以为你做智能体该做的事。对开发者来说这可能是老生常谈，因为他们早就下载过智能体并用了一段时间。但对大多数人来说，光是这个过渡过程就需要解释，需要非常用心地引导。当然，我们确实看到——因为我们用不同版本的模型做过测试，并持续做 AB 测试——产品体验对模型质量非常非常敏感。它非常依赖于模型能否可靠地完成这些任务，能否可靠地与用户沟通，能否在需要指导时可靠地回访用户。

turns.en: But how'd you know it was ready to be released?
turns.zh: 但你怎么知道它已经准备好发布了？

turns.en: Part of it was pretty numerical, which is like we had set—you go back to that spreadsheet of 100 plus things. We had set for each of those rows what threshold is launch blocking and above what threshold is good. We had many checkpoints that were green on 80 of the rows but red on 20 of the rows. We knew that wasn't good enough. And we had our first model checkpoint which was green across the board, which was a specially trained version of Musepark 1.3. So there was the very numerical part of it and then there was just the experiential part which is we tried the model. We could tell that it was a lot better than anything we had iterated with before.
turns.zh: 一部分是相当数字化的，比如我们设定——回到那个有 100 多项的表格。我们为每一行设定了什么阈值是阻碍发布的，高于什么阈值是好的。我们有很多检查点，在 80 行上是绿的，但在 20 行上是红的。我们知道那还不够好。然后我们有了第一个全绿的模型检查点，那是一个特别训练的 Musepark 1.3 版本。所以有非常数字化的部分，然后就是体验部分，我们试用了模型，能感觉到它比我们之前迭代过的任何版本都好得多。

turns.en: So going back to that seven-month period you were talking about, how many people were working on the product between the model work and the product work?
turns.zh: 那么回到你提到的那七个月，有多少人在做这个产品，包括模型工作和产品工作？

turns.en: Like under 200 people total, which I guess sounds like a lot, but in big company land it's actually a lot smaller. It's not very many. That was kind of cool looking back on this and thinking about it is like we knew this was going to be the most important product that the whole executive team, everyone knew that this was probably going to be one of the most important products that Meta would ship this year, but we had the restraint organizationally I think to make sure that it was a really small focused team working on it and that it didn't balloon to this like oh you have huge swaths of the company working on because we knew it was a single work of art. It required strong point of view and strong focus to pull that through into one beautiful experience.
turns.zh: 总共不到 200 人，听起来可能很多，但在大公司里其实小得多。人并不多。回头看这很酷，我们当时就知道这将是整个高管团队最重要的产品，每个人都知道这可能是 Meta 今年推出的最重要的产品之一，但我们在组织上有克制，确保是一个真正小而专注的团队在做，没有膨胀成让公司大片区域都参与进来，因为我们知道这是一件单一的艺术品。它需要强烈的观点和专注，才能把它打造成一个美好的体验。

turns.en: Say more about this. Why did you just call it like a single piece of art and you need a single perspective or point of view?
turns.zh: 多说说这个。为什么你称它为一件单一的艺术品，需要单一的视角或观点？

turns.en: I think one criticism of products that come from larger organizations and I think this is even now starting to plague a lot of the AI labs is that they become kind of this Frankenstein almost like Cronenberg amalgamation of a bunch of different people's points of view and visions and beliefs and it's sort of like it's sort of PM hell in some sense where every PM has a thing that they're trying to get into the product and jam into the product and then all that kind of blends together into this smoothie almost. People feel it as users and consumers—you can feel when a product is just like it feels like lots of different people worked on it and there were clearly different people who were gold differently so they just kind of jammed it all together. Muse had to be the exact opposite, which is like there's one clear point of view. There is one cohesive experience that we're trying to deliver to the world.
turns.zh: 我认为对来自大型组织的产品的一个批评，而且现在也开始困扰很多 AI 实验室，就是它们变成了弗兰肯斯坦式的、几乎像柯南伯格式的混合体，融合了一堆不同人的观点、愿景和信念，某种程度上像是产品经理的地狱，每个产品经理都想把自己的东西塞进产品里，然后所有这些混合成一杯冰沙。作为用户和消费者你能感觉到——当一个产品感觉像是很多不同的人做的，明显有不同的人各自为政，只是把它们拼凑在一起。Muse 必须完全相反，即有一个清晰的观点。我们试图向世界传递一个连贯的体验。

turns.en: I love that you said that and it just happens to be pure coincidence. Like we're—I don't know when this is going to come out, but we're recording this on the 15th anniversary of Steve Jobs' death. And when you think of somebody like a pro consumer products that had a single point of view, you obviously think of Steve first. I've read every single book on Steve and the history of Apple and I've done like I don't know 15 or 20 episodes on them for my other podcast Founders, but one of my favorite lines to describe Steve's impact was it says that Apple is just Steve Jobs with 10,000 lives. The products are to his taste, his perspective, his point of view. What he wanted to see in the world is exactly what the end user got. In Muse's case, Nat Friedman deserves a lot of credit. His taste and sensibilities ultimately dictated and shaped what that product became.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你这么说，而这纯属巧合。我们——我不知道这期什么时候播出，但我们是在史蒂夫·乔布斯逝世 15 周年纪念日录制的。当你想到一个拥有单一观点的消费产品专家时，你显然首先想到史蒂夫。我读过所有关于史蒂夫和苹果历史的书，为我的另一个播客《Founders》做了大概 15 到 20 期关于他们的节目，但我最喜欢的一句描述史蒂夫影响的话是：苹果就是史蒂夫·乔布斯的一万条命。产品符合他的品味、他的视角、他的观点。他想在世界中看到的东西，正是最终用户得到的。在 Muse 的案例中，Nat Friedman 值得很多赞誉。他的品味和感受力最终决定并塑造了那个产品。

turns.zh: 你们会谈论有多少人在用 Muse 吗？你们公开谈论这个吗？

Like for most people, there's just so they're just like constantly being like like kind of bombarded with new AI products and startups and releases and things and models and here's another model and here's another product and here's another feature and it's just like this torrential stream. turns.zh: 是的。你在你写的那篇帖子里说过，它很短，我记得上次看到它已经有 550 万次浏览了，但你说，嗯，我喜欢你描述 Muse 的方式，就像如果每个人都有一个超越自身的第二大脑。我认为从哲学上讲，这是最有趣的问题之一：当你拥有强大的 AI 时，作为人类意味着什么？这种关系是怎样的？它究竟会是什么样子？不同的人对它的样子有不同的看法。我想那种恐惧的情况，显然你知道 AI 在我们之上，我们只是在做它们做的事，还有其他世界，那种关系是不同的。但在你继续之前，你个人的观点是什么？

turns.en: I really believe in Muse. I believe in the personal agent as a long-term form factor of just it is human nature to have wants and desires and dreams. And I think AI and personal agents like Muse will be the mechanism and the bridge that enables us to accomplish those things and continue accomplishing them. And then humans will dream bigger and bigger and bigger and bigger. Kids will dream of having their own star systems or whatever. And Muse will help them do that. There's this thing that Bezos wrote in, well I think it was one of his shareholder letters, which is like the beautiful thing about consumers is that they're always beautifully unhappy or something like that, or beautifully unsatisfied with the options they have. That is one modality of our relationship with AI. I think that there's other modalities like I think that AI will start doing more and more of the scientific discovery process. I think AIs will start inserting more and more into various parts of the economy, but I do believe in this form factor long term of everyone having an AI that supports them and what they want.
turns.zh: 我真的相信 Muse。我相信个人智能体作为一种长期形态，因为拥有欲望、渴望和梦想是人性。我认为 AI 和像 Muse 这样的个人智能体将成为机制和桥梁，使我们能够实现这些目标并继续实现它们。然后人类会梦想得越来越大。孩子们会梦想拥有自己的星系之类的。Muse 会帮助他们做到这一点。贝索斯曾写过，我想是在他的一封股东信里，他说消费者的美妙之处在于他们总是美妙地不满足，或者类似的话，或者对他们拥有的选择美妙地不满意。这是我们与 AI 关系的一种模式。我认为还有其他模式，比如 AI 将开始越来越多地参与科学发现过程。AI 将开始越来越多地插入经济的各个部分，但我确实相信这种长期形态，即每个人都拥有一个支持他们及其愿望的 AI。

turns.en: So you see AI as kind of like removing all the cludge of life, right? The stuff that we don't want to do. I think in the piece you said something like the world is full of gatekeepers and obstacles and like Muse can get around this for you without spending any more of your time so you can actually focus on the stuff you want to do. I think Muse can give everyone the adulthood they dreamed of in childhood. Everyone when they're kids, they have big ideas and big dreams and when they imagine their life and they sort of play it out. They imagine this life where they can be an astronaut or they can save the planet or they can change the world or, you know, whatever it might be. It's like a big they think big and then for, you know, a variety of reasons by the time people finish school, they enter the workforce, by the time they get to their, you know, have been in a job for a while, it's that like all that hope and ambition and ability to dream has been sucked out of them.
turns.zh: 所以你认为 AI 能消除生活中的所有累赘，对吧？那些我们不想做的事情。我记得你在文章里说过，世界充满了守门人和障碍，Muse 可以帮你绕过这些，而不必花费你更多时间，这样你就能真正专注于你想做的事情。我认为 Muse 可以给每个人他们童年梦想的成年生活。每个人小时候都有宏大的想法和梦想，当他们想象自己的生活并演绎出来时，他们想象自己能成为宇航员，或者拯救地球，或者改变世界，或者随便什么。他们想得很大，然后由于各种原因，当人们完成学业、进入职场、工作一段时间后，所有的希望、雄心和梦想的能力都被抽走了。

turns.en: No, it's been beaten out of them. The life is beaten out of them. I think as adults, I don't think we appreciate the degree to which we're all zombies. We lost our agency and we lost our, I think ambition is really a good word for it. One of the promises of AI broadly speaking and I think through products like Muse is to keep it going from when you're a kid. Like you're a kid, you have big dreams, use AI, help make those things happen. Then dream bigger, make those things happen, dream bigger, make those things happen. And kind of experience this escalator of agency, an increase in agency throughout your life versus a sort of like you have lots of agency and then it gets crushed. You know what I was thinking of when you were speaking just now? You mentioned earlier this experience that you and Nat Freeman went through where you had this disturbing psychological audit and like coming in waves from this AI. It's like yeah, what if we had that but it's like the opposite of what you're saying. It's like actually gave you more self-confidence like gave you understanding like the world is malleable and if you push on it hard enough you go after it with enough energy and drive you can actually change it around you.
turns.zh: 不，是被打出来的。生活被打出来了。我认为作为成年人，我们并不欣赏我们都在多大程度上是僵尸。我们失去了能动性，失去了——我认为雄心是一个很好的词。广义上讲，AI 的承诺之一，我认为通过像 Muse 这样的产品，就是让你从孩提时代就保持这种状态。就像你是个孩子，你有大梦想，使用 AI，帮助实现这些。然后梦想更大，实现它们，梦想更大，实现它们。并体验这种能动性的自动扶梯，一生中能动性不断增加，而不是像你有很多能动性然后被压碎。你知道我刚才听你说话时在想什么吗？你之前提到你和 Nat Freeman 经历的那次令人不安的心理审计，像来自 AI 的波浪一样。就像，如果我们有那种，但与你说的相反。它实际上给了你更多自信，让你理解世界是可塑的，如果你足够用力推动它，用足够的能量和动力去追求它，你实际上可以改变周围的世界。

turns.en: Yeah. I think this is something that certainly the most impressive entrepreneurs exhibit which is like I think they like dream big they accomplish that then they dream bigger and then maybe they work on that for like a decade but then like you know if they accomplish that then they dream bigger. Like Elon is obviously a great example of this. I think Mark is a great example of this. I think but I think a lot of like the iconic entrepreneurs this is like kind of like their lived experience and I think there's a version of that that should be true for every person and I think what's kind of like tragic is I think for most people you have like bigger dreams big ideas you enter the corporate workforce you're you kind of become a zombie maybe at some point you want to go tackle your dreams but then it's like really really hard cuz you all these commitments. You maybe you have a family, maybe you have whatever it is. It's just like it's almost you become trapped in the sort of like zombiehood. There's one more thing on Muse before I want to get to Scale AI and like the partnership that you do that you did with Meta and making that decision. But in this essay that you wrote or this like short postage you wrote, I love what you said. said, "The world until now has been shaped by the small number of fanatics who have somehow found a way to make their wants real, but we've never seen humanity with every single person's agency fully switched on." I think the promise of this world that I'm describing where every single person has this like agency increase throughout their lifetime and they have the ability to accomplish their wants and their dreams. I think that world looks crazy in a very good way. Like I think it will be very interesting.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这是最令人印象深刻的企业家所展现的，他们梦想远大，实现它，然后梦想更大，也许为此工作十年，但如果实现了，他们就会梦想更大。埃隆显然是一个很好的例子。马克也是一个很好的例子。我认为很多标志性企业家都有这样的亲身经历，我认为应该有一个版本对每个人都适用。我认为有点悲剧的是，对大多数人来说，你有更大的梦想、宏大的想法，进入企业工作，你有点变成僵尸，也许某个时候你想去追求梦想，但那时真的很难，因为你有各种承诺。也许你有家庭，也许你有这样那样的事情。你几乎被困在僵尸状态中。在我想谈 Scale AI 以及你与 Meta 的合作和做出那个决定之前，关于 Muse 还有一件事。但在你写的这篇文章或短帖中，我喜欢你说的：“迄今为止，世界是由少数狂热者塑造的，他们以某种方式找到了实现自己愿望的方法，但我们从未见过人类每一个人的能动性都被完全开启。”我认为我所描述的这个世界的承诺，即每个人一生中能动性不断增加，有能力实现自己的愿望和梦想。我认为那个世界以一种非常好的方式看起来很疯狂。我觉得它会非常有趣。

turns.en: It'll be artistic and cool, and you'll go into different pockets of the world, and it will be very diverse. It'll be kind of insane to think about what exactly that looks like, where literally billions of people have, all of a sudden, because of abundant intelligence, the resources to make incredible things happen. I think that's part of the promise. In my head, it's almost like the Rick and Morty interdimensional cable, but somehow manifested into reality for humans. It could just be really awesome. So I keep hearing this line from that show where it's like, the universe eats smart people.
turns.zh: 它会充满艺术感、很酷，你会进入世界的不同角落，非常多元。很难想象那具体会是什么样子：数十亿人突然因为智能的极大丰富，拥有了让不可思议的事情发生的资源。我认为这是承诺的一部分。在我脑海里，这几乎就像《瑞克和莫蒂》里的跨维度电视，但不知怎么地变成了人类的现实。那可能会非常棒。所以我一直听到那部剧里的一句话，大意是“宇宙会吞噬聪明人”。

turns.en: Okay, so I want to go back. What I'm personally curious about is: you founded Scale AI, you're running Scale AI, and then one day Mark Zuckerberg reaches out and says, 'Hey,' I assume he says, 'Hey, I want to talk. Can you tell me about this?'
turns.zh: 好，我想回溯一下。我个人好奇的是：你创立了 Scale AI，你在经营 Scale AI，然后有一天马克·扎克伯格联系你说，“嘿，”我猜他说的是，“嘿，我想聊聊。你能跟我讲讲这个吗？”

turns.en: Yeah, I think the exact message was something like, 'Hey, do you have time for a call?'
turns.zh: 是的，我想那条消息大概是：“嘿，你有时间通个电话吗？”

turns.en: Did you have a relationship with Mark previously? Did you spend any time with him? What was the background there?
turns.zh: 你之前和马克有交情吗？你和他有过接触吗？背景是怎样的？

turns.en: I had a friend, this guy Alex Schultz, who I've known for many, many years, from when Scale was maybe a year old. I met him in San Francisco. He is currently the chief data officer at Meta, but was a longtime Meta executive lieutenant, and he introduced me to Mark, I want to say in about 2021 or 2022, to talk about AI, because at that time Mark was getting a lot more interested in AI. Scale was doing a lot of stuff in AI. My memory is that it took like 1 year to schedule that first meeting. From the intro to the meeting being scheduled, I think it was like a full year.
turns.zh: 我有一个朋友，叫亚历克斯·舒尔茨，我认识他很多很多年了，那时 Scale 可能才成立一年。我在旧金山认识他。他目前是 Meta 的首席数据官，但曾是 Meta 的长期高管亲信。他把我介绍给马克，我想大概是在 2021 年或 2022 年，为了聊 AI，因为那时马克对 AI 越来越感兴趣。Scale 在 AI 方面做了很多事。我记得安排那第一次会面花了大约一年。从介绍到会议安排，我想整整一年。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: Mark obviously has an insane calendar and has a bajillion different things to deal with. And he's also very good at prioritization. He will spend a lot of time on the things that are really, really important—in some ways, too much time on the things that are really, really important. The only way he's able to do that and be a good dad and a good partner and all this other stuff is to just ruthlessly prioritize. I had spoken to him a few times after that and had gotten his advice as a founder—to get advice from Mark Zuckerberg is obviously a really big deal. I actually remember at that time he wrote these—I would ask him a question on WhatsApp and then he would write these really long responses and I was really confused. I was like, how does he have time to write these really long responses? But now I realize he is just really fast and rigorous at writing a lot of WhatsApp messages. He'll write a very rigorous, long response very quickly. It's a very impressive skill of his.
turns.zh: 马克显然日程排得极满，有无数事情要处理。他也非常擅长排优先级。他会花大量时间在真正重要的事情上——某种程度上，在真正重要的事情上花的时间过多。他能做到这一点，同时还能当个好爸爸、好伴侣等等，唯一的方法就是无情地排优先级。在那之后我和他聊过几次，作为创始人得到他的建议——能得到马克·扎克伯格的建议显然是件大事。我 actually 记得那时他会写——我在 WhatsApp 上问他一个问题，然后他会写很长的回复，我当时很困惑。我想，他怎么有时间写这么长的回复？但现在我意识到，他只是写大量 WhatsApp 消息时又快又严谨。他能很快写出非常严谨的长回复。这是他一项非常令人印象深刻的技能。

turns.en: Gives you a sneak peek into what's going on in his mind.
turns.zh: 让你窥见他脑子里在想什么。

turns.en: Yeah. Meta was an important customer of Scale. I would say prior to this instance, maybe we spoke once every six months or so. Maybe that was the cadence of our interactions. And then yeah, I think he had called and I think it was actually not obvious at first what the end point was going to be, because the first conversation was just like, you know, this was after Llama 4 and it was kind of just asking, what do you think we should be doing?
turns.zh: 是的。Meta 是 Scale 的重要客户。我想说在这件事之前，我们大概每六个月聊一次。也许那就是我们互动的频率。然后是的，我想他打了电话，一开始其实并不清楚最终会走向什么，因为第一次对话就像，你知道，那是在 Llama 4 之后，基本上就是问，你觉得我们应该做什么？

turns.en: Why is that an important point that this conversation is happening after Llama 4?
turns.zh: 为什么这次对话发生在 Llama 4 之后是一个重要的点？

turns.en: Llama 4 was not on the trajectory that Meta wanted as a company. It definitely was, internally speaking, a disappointment, and it was also at a time where AI was clearly becoming increasingly important. It was clear that AI was going to be really critical to the future of Meta. So yeah, the first few conversations we spoke on the phone and he was sort of asking for advice on, what do you think we should be doing? What do you think we should be focused on? This is what I've heard about him privately: that he has this insane—it's not a board of directors, like a Meta board, although there are some people on the board that he also does this with—but he's got this group of world-class entrepreneurs around him, and I've spoken to some of them, like, you don't understand, he asks for advice constantly. He's hitting us up, like, here's what's going on in my life or the work, what would you do? And he'll do that over and over and over again. I think this is quite an impressive trait, because it takes humility, obviously, to continue doing that even after all the incredible things he's been able to accomplish. I mean, the whole timeline from when he first reached out to when we announced the deal was like five, six weeks. It was pretty quick.
turns.zh: Llama 4 没有走在 Meta 作为一家公司想要的轨迹上。内部来说，它肯定令人失望，而且当时 AI 显然正变得越来越重要。很明显，AI 对 Meta 的未来至关重要。所以是的，最初几次对话我们通电话，他有点像是在征求建议：你觉得我们应该做什么？你觉得我们应该聚焦什么？这是我私下听说的关于他的事：他有一个疯狂的——不是董事会，不是 Meta 董事会，虽然董事会里有些人他也会这样——但他身边有一群世界级的企业家，我和其中一些人聊过，他们说，你不明白，他不断地征求建议。他会找我们，说，这是我生活中或工作上正在发生的事，你会怎么做？他会一遍又一遍地这样做。我认为这是一个相当令人钦佩的特质，因为显然需要谦逊，才能在取得了所有这些不可思议的成就之后还继续这样做。我是说，从他第一次联系到我们宣布交易，整个时间线大概五、六周。相当快。

turns.en: Another thing that world-class entrepreneurs have in common. We had Jonathan Ross, the founder of Groq, on this podcast. The first time we ever spoke publicly about the $20 billion deal he did with Nvidia was on the show. And he's like, from the time of the first call from Jensen to money's in my bank account was 3 weeks.
turns.zh: 世界级企业家的另一个共同点。我们请过 Groq 的创始人乔纳森·罗斯上这个播客。他第一次公开谈论他与英伟达达成的 200 亿美元交易就是在本节目上。他说，从黄仁勋第一次打电话到钱到我银行账户，只用了 3 周。

turns.en: Yeah. That's amazing. I just had lots of ideas on what I'd be doing if I choose and how I'd be thinking about Meta's AI strategy. One of the first things I said was what I said earlier, which is, hey, I actually think because Meta is, heritage-wise, focused on the things that people want to do, it is actually one of the most specially placed companies with this incredible shift in AI. I had lots and lots of ideas that I sent his way, and then that was kind of this conversation happening in parallel with this, oh yeah, maybe we should potentially consider if there's a way to work together.
turns.zh: 是的。太厉害了。我有很多想法，关于如果我选择的话我会做什么，以及我会如何思考 Meta 的 AI 战略。我最早说的话之一就是我之前说的：嘿，我 actually 认为，因为 Meta 在传承上专注于人们想做的事，它实际上是这次 AI 巨大转变中处于最特殊位置的公司之一。我有很多很多想法发给了他，然后那场对话与这个并行发生：哦对，也许我们应该考虑一下是否有办法合作。

turns.en: So when he says that, what do you think? Because this kid—you—this was not predictable to you.
turns.zh: 所以当他说那个的时候，你怎么想？因为这小子——你——这对你来说不可预测。

turns.en: Not predictable. No. The whole thing was a really crazy sequence at the time. I was just like, oh, that's nice, but there's no way that—
turns.zh: 不可预测。不。整件事在当时是一连串非常疯狂的经过。我当时就想，哦，那挺好，但绝不可能——

turns.en: Well, you know what that means when they say that, right? They want to buy you. It's always the same thing, but they say it's like, oh, we got to find a way to work together.
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道他们这么说意味着什么，对吧？他们想收购你。总是同一套，但他们说成，哦，我们得找到一种合作的方式。

turns.en: Yeah. I don't think I'd had that kind of coaching at the time.
turns.zh: 是的。我想我当时没有受过那种指导。

turns.en: One thing that I explicitly felt at the time was like, yeah, it probably doesn't make that much sense even. I personally was like, maybe he's teasing it or throwing it out there, but does he even make that much sense?
turns.zh: 当时我明确感觉到的一件事是，嗯，这甚至可能不太合理。我个人当时想，也许他只是在开玩笑或者随便说说，但这真的合理吗？

turns.en: Why wouldn't you think it makes sense?
turns.zh: 为什么你会觉得它不合理？

turns.en: I mean, obviously a deal ended up happening, so what do I know? But
turns.zh: 我的意思是，显然最终交易达成了，所以我知道什么呢？但是

turns.en: No, no, but back then, not we know what happened, but I'm very curious your thinking as you're going experiencing this like the fact that you said, oh, yeah, you said this was like that doesn't make sense. Like why wouldn't it make sense?
turns.zh: 不，不，但当时，不是我们现在知道发生了什么，但我很好奇你当时的想法，因为你说过，哦，你说这好像不合理。为什么它不合理？

turns.en: Taking a step back. Obviously the iconic Meta acquisitions have been Instagram and WhatsApp and these were very clear product logic driven decisions. Scale is like a deep enterprise government sales, an entirely different kind of business from Meta. And so the logic that I had thought at the time would have made sense is if Meta wanted to get into those things, then maybe that's the industrial logic that would have made sense, but this wasn't that because I think Mark clearly was predominantly interested in getting the Llama program and his overall AI program on
turns.zh: 退一步说。显然，Meta 的标志性收购是 Instagram 和 WhatsApp，这些都是非常明确的产品逻辑驱动的决策。Scale 是深度企业政府销售，与 Meta 完全不同的业务。所以当时我认为合理的逻辑是，如果 Meta 想进入这些领域，那么也许那是合理的产业逻辑，但这次不是，因为我认为马克主要感兴趣的是获得 Llama 项目和整体 AI 项目

turns.en: He wanted talent.
turns.zh: 他想要人才。

turns.en: Yeah he wanted talent. It was kind of shrouded and unclear the whole time, a lot of the way.
turns.zh: 是的，他想要人才。整个过程在很多方面都有些模糊不清。

turns.en: When did it become clear?
turns.zh: 什么时候变得清晰？

turns.en: After the money hit the account when we started talking numbers, I was like, oh, wow. Okay. All right. That's when things became more clear.
turns.zh: 当钱到账后，我们开始谈数字时，我心想，哦，哇。好的。好吧。那时事情变得更清晰了。

turns.en: At first, you're like, oh, this will make sense. Then you guys keep talking. And how fast did he convince you like this is a good path for you?
turns.zh: 起初，你觉得，哦，这会有道理。然后你们继续谈。他多快说服你这是一条好路？

turns.en: There was a part of it was just like, wow, this is like a really fascinating deal construct. We ultimately landed on this deal where Meta invested, owns 49% of Scale, Scale continues. Myself and a few people join Meta. What I was kind of incredulous about at the time was like it's such a weird kind of deal but is one that I think genuinely was like this very interesting win-win-win so to speak. turns.zh: 听众们不知道我刚才指的是什么？你能快速说一下你 19 岁生日派对上都有谁，以及为什么如果当时投资了桌边的每个人，那会是一笔好赌注？

turns.en: This is like a really crazy thing to think about. my 19th birthday party. I was a freshman at MIT. It was in January. I was doing a win internship, a winter internship, win internship at a trading firm called HRT. There were like 10 of us, 12 of us, um, something like that. Almost all of whom were students at either Harvard or MIT. Most of us already knew each other from various math and science or computer science competitions. Some of the other people were Jeffrey Yan who went on to start Hyperlquid very successful. Um Scott Wu went on to start Cognition very successful. Another person there was uh uh Jesse Zang went to start Decagon also quite successful. Um another person was Vicky Yei who is I think a brilliant researcher works at Anthropic. Everyone was like incredibly talented. I actually talked to the uh the founder of HRT recently and HRT itself by the way now is like crushing it. Unbelievable.
turns.zh: 这真是想想都觉得疯狂。我 19 岁生日派对。我当时是 MIT 的新生。那是一月份。我在一家叫 HRT 的交易公司做冬季实习。我们大概有 10 个人，12 个人，差不多这样。几乎所有人都是哈佛或 MIT 的学生。我们大多数人已经在各种数学、科学或计算机科学竞赛中认识了。其他人包括 Jeffrey Yan，后来创办了 Hyperliquid，非常成功。Scott Wu 后来创办了 Cognition，非常成功。还有 Jesse Zhang 创办了 Decagon，也相当成功。另一个人是 Vicky Yei，我认为她是一位杰出的研究员，在 Anthropic 工作。每个人都才华横溢。我最近实际上和 HRT 的创始人谈过，HRT 本身现在也做得非常好。难以置信。

turns.en: What does HRT do?
turns.zh: HRT 是做什么的？

turns.en: HRT it's a proprietary trading firm. So they they trade their own money in Q2 of um 6 had 11 billion of revenue and like I think 8 billion of profit is the the record number. This is a I think it's under a thousand people work at HRT. I mean, it's like unbelievable. But I I recently uh met up with the founder of HRT and they were talking about like, "Oh yeah, we're starting to do some private investments." I was like, "Just invest into the interns. All the interns get seed checks." That's great.
turns.zh: HRT 是一家自营交易公司。他们用自己的钱交易，在 2026 年第二季度有 110 亿营收，我记得利润是 80 亿，创纪录的数字。HRT 的员工不到一千人。我的意思是，这简直难以置信。但我最近和 HRT 的创始人见面，他们谈到：“哦，我们开始做一些私人投资了。”我说：“就投资实习生吧。所有实习生都拿种子轮支票。”那很棒。

turns.en: I grew up doing uh math and uh science and computer science competitions and Olympiads and got to know like all sorts of people from all around America doing this kind of stuff. It's like quite surreal to see the people that I did competitions with become so successful.
turns.zh: 我从小参加数学、科学和计算机科学竞赛和奥林匹克竞赛，认识了来自美国各地做这类事情的各种人。看到和我一起参加竞赛的人变得如此成功，真是超现实。

turns.en: It's going to be fascinating what all of you do the next few decades. Before I interrupted you, did you have more to say about diamond mining and skyscraper stuff?
turns.zh: 你们所有人在未来几十年会做什么，将会非常引人入胜。在我打断你之前，关于钻石开采和摩天大楼的事情你还有更多要说的吗？

turns.en: Basically, it's like does it have a power law payoff where some things just like pay for like literally like a million times the investment or is it something more like building skyscrapers which I would I would describe data annotation or or or data businesses as more like this which is like Amazon Prime deliveries is another example where the payoff is pretty linear and you have to just get develop a process where you're like really really amazing at doing it. If you're building skyscrapers, then it's like a very operational business and it's all about like squeezing every ounce of efficiency out of that process and you just look at it and you figure out like I can make it like 2% more efficient this way and 1% more efficient that way and half a percent more efficient that way and you just try to squeeze every ounce of optimization out of it. And then there's diamond mining where you're kind of like, "Hey everyone, just like you know, go forth, try all your crazy ideas and like you're just nurturing the ideas that seem promising."
turns.zh: 基本上，就是看它是否有幂律回报，有些东西的回报 literally 是投资的一百万倍，还是更像建造摩天大楼，我会把数据标注或数据业务描述为更像这种，就像亚马逊 Prime 配送是另一个例子，回报相当线性，你必须开发一个流程，让你非常非常擅长做这件事。如果你在建造摩天大楼，那是一个非常运营性的业务，关键是从过程中榨取每一分效率，你看着它，想办法让这边效率提高 2%，那边提高 1%，另一边提高 0.5%，你试图榨取每一分优化。然后是钻石开采，你就像是，“嘿大家，去尝试所有疯狂的想法，培育那些看起来有前途的想法。”

turns.en: That's what you feel you're doing at Meta right now.
turns.zh: 这就是你觉得你现在在 Meta 做的事情。

turns.en: That's what I feel I'm doing at Meta. And and and the building server stuff generally speaking is what I felt I was doing at at scale. And that's like this big paradigm um paradigm difference.
turns.zh: 这就是我觉得我在 Meta 做的事情。而建造服务器之类的事情，一般来说是我觉得我在 Scale 做的事情。这是一个巨大的范式差异。

turns.en: Going back to the coaching and the way the difference of how you're essentially managing now at meta compared to way scale. Why do you have so many direct reports? You have like what 100 direct reports? How many direct reports?
turns.zh: 回到 coaching 以及你现在在 Meta 的管理方式与 Scale 相比的差异。为什么你有这么多直接下属？你有大概 100 个直接下属？有多少直接下属？

turns.en: Yeah, I think more than 200. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我想超过 200 个。是的。

turns.en: How and why? Going back to one of the founding theses of MSL and what we want to do and rebuilding this lab, how do you have really, really high talent density? How do you make it the best place for a lot of these brilliant people to do their best work, and how do you build an organization that's technically focused where the technical people are doing their best work, have the opportunity to really do their life's work?
turns.zh: 如何以及为什么？回到 MSL 的创始论点之一，以及我们想做什么、重建这个实验室，你如何实现非常非常高的人才密度？你如何让它成为许多这些杰出人才做出最佳工作的最佳场所，以及你如何建立一个技术聚焦的组织，让技术人员做他们最好的工作，有机会真正做他们一生的工作？

turns.en: And one of the design principles around this was making it very flat. Effectively all the researchers that we hired into this group called TBD, they report directly to me. And it's more of a statement of the fact that this is anti-bureaucracy. TBD is literally anti-bureaucracy. The point is we're hiring brilliant people and you all have demonstrated clearly that you can do brilliant, brilliant work. You have done it before in your careers. So I don't need to be micromanaging you to do brilliant work. You're going to be able to do that on your own. We need technical leadership. So, some of you are going to be responsible for setting clear technical directions for your groups and we have this kind of pod structure where we have various pods and there's various technical leads of the pods who tie break on the technical decisions. So, there's a technical leadership structure in place, but from a quote unquote people management perspective or from a bureaucracy perspective, we're just anti-bureaucracy.
turns.zh: 其中一个设计原则是让它非常扁平。实际上，我们招进这个叫 TBD 的组的所有研究员都直接向我汇报。这更像是一种声明：这是反官僚的。TBD 字面上就是反官僚。关键是我们在招聘杰出人才，你们所有人都清楚地证明了自己能做出卓越的工作。你们在职业生涯中已经做到过。所以我不需要微观管理你们来做卓越的工作。你们自己就能做到。我们需要技术领导力。所以，你们中的一些人将负责为你们的组设定清晰的技术方向，我们有这种 pod 结构，有各种 pod，每个 pod 有技术负责人，他们在技术决策上做最终裁决。所以，有一个技术领导结构，但从所谓的人员管理角度或官僚角度，我们就是反官僚。

turns.en: And then the other part of this is we do make a lot of group decisions. We want to debate because it is a very talent dense group of brilliant people. We want to have those conversations where we're all discussing what we think the right path is. Everyone in the lab has done brilliant things. We want to hear all these opinions. We want to arrive at things that we all believe are the best path forward. So it's certainly an unconventional way to run the team. And I would be lying if I said I was the best manager to more than 200 people. But this part of the point is that they don't need managers, they need a great environment. They are all brilliant. They're all extremely capable. They just need the room to cook.
turns.zh: 然后另一部分是，我们确实做很多集体决策。我们想要辩论，因为这是一个人才密度极高的杰出群体。我们想要进行那些对话，大家一起讨论我们认为正确的路径是什么。实验室里的每个人都做过卓越的事情。我们想听到所有这些意见。我们想要达成我们都认为是前进最佳路径的共识。所以这确实是一种非常规的团队管理方式。如果我说我是管理 200 多人的最佳经理，那我就是在撒谎。但关键是他们不需要经理，他们需要一个伟大的环境。他们都很杰出。他们都极其有能力。他们只需要空间去发挥。

turns.en: Yeah. And so maybe not a coach. You're kind of like the steward of a great environment so they can do great work.
turns.zh: 是的。所以也许不是教练。你更像是伟大环境的管理者，这样他们就能做出伟大的工作。

turns.en: Yeah. Exactly.
turns.zh: 是的。没错。

turns.en: Alex, this was awesome, man. Thanks for taking the time.
turns.zh: Alex，这太棒了，伙计。感谢你抽出时间。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I hope you enjoyed this episode. Please remember to subscribe wherever you're listening and leave a review. And make sure you listen to my other podcast, Founders. For almost a decade, I've obsessively read over 400 biographies of history's greatest entrepreneurs, searching for ideas that you can use in your work. Most of the guests you hear on this show first found me through Founders.
turns.zh: 我希望你喜欢这一集。请记得在你收听的地方订阅并留下评论。并确保收听我的另一档播客《Founders》。近十年来，我痴迷地阅读了 400 多本历史上最伟大企业家的传记，寻找你可以在工作中使用的想法。你在这个节目中听到的大多数嘉宾都是通过《Founders》先找到我的。

consensus.en: Personal superintelligence is the mission: AI should lift human experience and amplify agency for everyone.
consensus.zh: 个人超级智能是使命：AI 应提升人类体验，放大每个人的能动性。

consensus.en: Meta is uniquely positioned for consumer AI because its products represent what people want to do.
consensus.zh: Meta 在消费级 AI 上具有独特优势，因为其产品代表人们想做的事。

consensus.en: Muse succeeded by relentlessly sanding details into a reliable, polished consumer product.
consensus.zh: Muse 的成功源于对细节的持续打磨，打造出可靠、精致的消费级产品。

consensus.en: Model quality and reliability are the core determinants of a personal agent product experience.
consensus.zh: 模型质量与可靠性是个人智能体产品体验的核心决定因素。

consensus.en: A small, flat, high-talent-density team can move faster than a large bureaucratic organization.
consensus.zh: 小而扁平、高人才密度的团队比大型官僚组织行动更快。

consensus.en: Great people need an environment where they can do their best work, not micromanagement.
consensus.zh: 优秀的人需要能发挥最佳水平的环境，而非微观管理。

contrarian.en: Coding agents are not the only form factor that matters; personal agents are the real consumer endpoint.
contrarian.zh: 编程智能体并非唯一重要的形态；个人智能体才是真正的消费级终点。

contrarian.en: Meta can win AI even when conventional wisdom says it cannot.
contrarian.zh: 即便主流观点认为 Meta 赢不了 AI，它依然可以赢。

contrarian.en: A single cohesive point of view beats a Frankenstein product built by many PMs.
contrarian.zh: 单一连贯的产品视角胜过由众多产品经理拼凑出的弗兰肯斯坦式产品。

contrarian.en: The internet rewards risk and surprise, so unhinged memes can genuinely drive growth.
contrarian.zh: 互联网奖励风险与惊喜，因此看似疯癫的梗图确实能推动增长。

contrarian.en: Most people don't care about your company or research; they only care what it does for them.
contrarian.zh: 大多数人不在乎你的公司或研究，只在乎它能为自己做什么。

contrarian.en: AI can restore the agency and ambition that adulthood beats out of people.
contrarian.zh: AI 可以恢复成年生活从人们身上磨灭的能动性与抱负。
